questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the endocrine pancreas from the exocrine pancreas?

choices.A: Endocrine islets release digestive enzymes, while exocrine tissue releases hormones into blood.
choices.B: Endocrine tissue forms most of the pancreas, while exocrine tissue forms only the islets.
choices.C: Endocrine and exocrine tissue both release their products through the same pancreatic duct.
choices.D: Endocrine islets release hormones into blood, while exocrine tissue releases digestive juice into the intestine.

questions.explanation: The pancreas is a mixed gland: its islets are endocrine, whereas its much larger exocrine portion delivers digestive secretions to the intestine.
questions.miniGuide: The pancreas is a mixed gland: its islets are endocrine, whereas its much larger exocrine portion delivers digestive secretions to the intestine.

questions.question: Which islet cell and hormone pairing is correct?

choices.C: Delta cell — amylin
choices.D: Alpha cell — insulin

questions.explanation: Alpha cells produce glucagon, beta cells produce insulin and amylin, and delta cells produce somatostatin.
questions.miniGuide: Alpha cells produce glucagon, beta cells produce insulin and amylin, and delta cells produce somatostatin.

questions.question: Why does close proximity among pancreatic islet cells matter?

choices.A: It permits local communication that coordinates hormone secretion.
choices.B: It makes all islet cells respond identically to glucose.
choices.C: It allows every islet hormone to enter the pancreatic duct.
choices.D: It prevents insulin from reaching the systemic circulation.

questions.explanation: Nearby alpha, beta, and delta cells influence one another through local signals, helping coordinate insulin, glucagon, and somatostatin release.
questions.miniGuide: Nearby alpha, beta, and delta cells influence one another through local signals, helping coordinate insulin, glucagon, and somatostatin release.

questions.question: Within the pancreatic islet, insulin directly inhibits secretion of which hormone?

choices.C: Growth hormone
choices.D: Thyroid hormone

questions.explanation: Beta-cell insulin locally restrains alpha-cell glucagon secretion as part of coordinated islet regulation.
questions.miniGuide: Beta-cell insulin locally restrains alpha-cell glucagon secretion as part of coordinated islet regulation.

questions.question: Which additional hormone is secreted by pancreatic beta cells?

choices.C: Amylin
choices.D: Somatostatin

questions.explanation: Beta cells release both insulin and amylin; amylin contributes to post-meal regulation.
questions.miniGuide: Beta cells release both insulin and amylin; amylin contributes to post-meal regulation.

questions.question: Somatostatin produced within the islet inhibits secretion of which pair?

choices.C: Cortisol and aldosterone
choices.D: Epinephrine and norepinephrine

questions.explanation: Delta-cell somatostatin acts locally as a brake on both major pancreatic metabolic hormones.
questions.miniGuide: Delta-cell somatostatin acts locally as a brake on both major pancreatic metabolic hormones.

questions.question: Which description best characterizes insulin?

choices.A: A steroid catabolic hormone from alpha cells
choices.B: A peptide anabolic hormone from beta cells
choices.C: A catecholamine anabolic hormone from delta cells
choices.D: A steroid inhibitory hormone from beta cells

questions.explanation: Insulin is a short-lived peptide hormone that promotes nutrient storage after eating and during growth.
questions.miniGuide: Insulin is a short-lived peptide hormone that promotes nutrient storage after eating and during growth.

questions.question: What is released when proinsulin is cleaved inside the beta cell?

choices.C: Insulin and C-peptide
choices.D: Insulin and glucagon

questions.explanation: Processing of proinsulin removes C-peptide and produces mature insulin for secretion.
questions.miniGuide: Processing of proinsulin removes C-peptide and produces mature insulin for secretion.

questions.question: What is the main stimulus for insulin secretion?

choices.C: Decreased amino acids
choices.D: Increased blood glucose

questions.explanation: Rising blood glucose after a meal is the primary stimulus for beta-cell insulin release.
questions.miniGuide: Rising blood glucose after a meal is the primary stimulus for beta-cell insulin release.

questions.question: Which glucose transporter allows glucose to enter the pancreatic beta cell in the lecture pathway?

choices.C: GLUT3
choices.D: GLUT4

questions.explanation: Glucose entry through beta-cell GLUT2 participates in coupling blood glucose levels to insulin secretion.
questions.miniGuide: Glucose entry through beta-cell GLUT2 participates in coupling blood glucose levels to insulin secretion.

questions.question: Which meal-related change can enhance insulin secretion in addition to glucose?

choices.C: Increased sympathetic inhibition
choices.D: Reduced plasma amino acids

questions.explanation: Increased amino acids, especially arginine and lysine, reinforce insulin secretion after a protein-containing meal.
questions.miniGuide: Increased amino acids, especially arginine and lysine, reinforce insulin secretion after a protein-containing meal.

questions.question: How do gastrointestinal hormones such as GIP and GLP-1 affect insulin release?

choices.A: They stimulate glucagon instead of insulin.
choices.B: They prevent beta cells from sensing glucose.
choices.C: They increase meal-related insulin secretion.
choices.D: They suppress insulin during nutrient absorption.

questions.explanation: Gastrointestinal hormones reinforce beta-cell secretion when nutrients enter the digestive tract.
questions.miniGuide: Gastrointestinal hormones reinforce beta-cell secretion when nutrients enter the digestive tract.

questions.question: Parasympathetic acetylcholine has what effect on insulin secretion?

choices.C: It increases secretion.
choices.D: It prevents glucose from entering beta cells.

questions.explanation: Parasympathetic input supports insulin release in association with feeding.
questions.miniGuide: Parasympathetic input supports insulin release in association with feeding.

questions.question: During sympathetic activation, insulin secretion generally does what?

choices.C: Changes into somatostatin secretion
choices.D: Increases without limit

questions.explanation: Sympathetic activity generally suppresses insulin secretion, helping preserve circulating glucose during stress.
questions.miniGuide: Sympathetic activity generally suppresses insulin secretion, helping preserve circulating glucose during stress.

questions.question: Which transporter mediates insulin-dependent glucose uptake in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue?

choices.C: SGLT1
choices.D: GLUT4

questions.explanation: Insulin moves GLUT4-containing vesicles to the membrane of skeletal muscle and adipose cells.
questions.miniGuide: Insulin moves GLUT4-containing vesicles to the membrane of skeletal muscle and adipose cells.

questions.question: Which transport pathway is insulin-independent?

choices.C: GLUT4 uptake in resting skeletal muscle
choices.D: Insulin-stimulated GLUT4 vesicle insertion

questions.explanation: GLUT1–3 support insulin-independent glucose transport, whereas GLUT4 is the major insulin-responsive transporter.
questions.miniGuide: GLUT1–3 support insulin-independent glucose transport, whereas GLUT4 is the major insulin-responsive transporter.

questions.question: What is a rapid effect of insulin-receptor stimulation?

choices.A: Conversion of alpha cells into beta cells
choices.B: Translocation of GLUT4-containing vesicles to the cell membrane
choices.C: Destruction of intracellular glucose transporters
choices.D: Production of new proteins through gene translation

questions.explanation: Within seconds, insulin increases surface GLUT4 and thereby increases glucose uptake in responsive tissues.
questions.miniGuide: Within seconds, insulin increases surface GLUT4 and thereby increases glucose uptake in responsive tissues.

questions.question: Which response represents a long-term rather than rapid effect of insulin?

choices.C: Immediate increase in glucose permeability
choices.D: Increased translation and production of new proteins

questions.explanation: Insulin's long-term effects occur over hours to days and include altered translation and new protein synthesis.
questions.miniGuide: Insulin's long-term effects occur over hours to days and include altered translation and new protein synthesis.

questions.question: When does skeletal-muscle glucose uptake increase most directly?

choices.A: During exercise or after insulin rises with a meal
choices.C: Only when glucagon activates GLUT4
choices.D: Only when blood glucose becomes dangerously low

questions.explanation: Exercise and post-meal insulin both increase skeletal-muscle glucose uptake by promoting GLUT4 movement to the membrane.
questions.miniGuide: Exercise and post-meal insulin both increase skeletal-muscle glucose uptake by promoting GLUT4 movement to the membrane.

questions.question: After a meal, unused glucose in skeletal muscle is primarily stored as what?

choices.C: Cholesterol
choices.D: Glycogen

questions.explanation: Insulin promotes uptake of meal-derived glucose and storage of the unused portion as muscle glycogen.
questions.miniGuide: Insulin promotes uptake of meal-derived glucose and storage of the unused portion as muscle glycogen.

questions.question: Which hepatic response is promoted by insulin?

choices.C: Glycogen breakdown and ketone formation
choices.D: Gluconeogenesis and glucose release

questions.explanation: In the liver, insulin favors glucose uptake, use, and storage while opposing glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis.
questions.miniGuide: In the liver, insulin favors glucose uptake, use, and storage while opposing glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis.

questions.question: What hormonal pattern is expected between meals?

choices.C: Both insulin and glucagon remain maximally elevated.
choices.D: Somatostatin permanently suppresses both hormones.

questions.explanation: Lower insulin and higher glucagon shift metabolism away from storage and toward maintenance of circulating fuel.
questions.miniGuide: Lower insulin and higher glucagon shift metabolism away from storage and toward maintenance of circulating fuel.

questions.question: Why does insulin have relatively little effect on glucose utilization by the brain?

choices.A: Brain cells use only fatty acids for energy.
choices.B: Brain cells express only insulin-dependent GLUT4.
choices.C: Brain glucose entry is largely insulin-independent.
choices.D: Brain cells cannot metabolize glucose.

questions.explanation: Brain cells are already permeable to glucose, which makes severe hypoglycemia especially dangerous to neural function.
questions.miniGuide: Brain cells are already permeable to glucose, which makes severe hypoglycemia especially dangerous to neural function.

questions.question: How does insulin promote triglyceride storage in adipose tissue?

choices.A: It stimulates ketone release from adipocytes.
choices.B: It blocks glucose entry and increases lipolysis.
choices.C: It removes glycerol needed for triglyceride formation.
choices.D: It provides glucose for triglyceride synthesis.

questions.explanation: Adipose glucose metabolism supplies glycerol for triglyceride formation, supporting insulin's fat-storing effect.
questions.miniGuide: Adipose glucose metabolism supplies glycerol for triglyceride formation, supporting insulin's fat-storing effect.

questions.question: Why is insulin described as a “fat sparer”?

choices.A: It increases hormone-sensitive lipase and lipolysis.
choices.B: It blocks glucose use so tissues must oxidize fat.
choices.C: It inhibits fat breakdown and promotes fat storage.
choices.D: It converts all fatty acids into ketone bodies.

questions.explanation: Insulin inhibits adipose lipase, promotes glucose entry, and favors triglyceride formation rather than mobilization.
questions.miniGuide: Insulin inhibits adipose lipase, promotes glucose entry, and favors triglyceride formation rather than mobilization.

questions.question: How can severe insulin deficiency lead to metabolic acidosis?

choices.A: It forces all tissues to store triglycerides.
choices.B: It accelerates lipolysis and hepatic ketone formation.
choices.C: It increases glucose storage until blood glucose falls.
choices.D: It prevents fatty acids from entering the blood.

questions.explanation: Without insulin, stored fat is mobilized, free fatty acids become major fuels, and excess hepatic ketogenesis can cause acidosis.
questions.miniGuide: Without insulin, stored fat is mobilized, free fatty acids become major fuels, and excess hepatic ketogenesis can cause acidosis.

questions.question: Which action allows insulin to promote protein storage?

choices.C: Increasing amino-acid uptake and protein synthesis
choices.D: Increasing urea loss and protein breakdown

questions.explanation: Insulin moves amino acids into cells, supports translation, and inhibits protein catabolism.
questions.miniGuide: Insulin moves amino acids into cells, supports translation, and inhibits protein catabolism.

questions.question: Which outcome follows prolonged insulin deficiency?

choices.A: Protein wasting with increased amino acids and urea
choices.B: Increased protein storage and reduced urea formation
choices.C: Increased amino-acid uptake and reduced catabolism
choices.D: Increased protein synthesis and reduced gluconeogenesis

questions.explanation: Insulin deficiency removes anabolic support, increasing protein breakdown, circulating amino acids, and urinary urea.
questions.miniGuide: Insulin deficiency removes anabolic support, increasing protein breakdown, circulating amino acids, and urinary urea.

questions.question: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, which metabolic shift best reflects insulin's overall action?

choices.A: From glycogen synthesis toward glycogen breakdown
choices.B: From nutrient mobilization toward nutrient use and storage
choices.C: From protein synthesis toward protein catabolism
choices.D: From glucose use toward ketone production

questions.explanation: Insulin acts as a metabolic switch that favors carbohydrate use and storage of glucose, fat, and protein after feeding.
questions.miniGuide: Insulin acts as a metabolic switch that favors carbohydrate use and storage of glucose, fat, and protein after feeding.

questions.question: Which condition most strongly stimulates glucagon secretion?

choices.C: High blood glucose after a meal
choices.D: High insulin during nutrient storage

questions.explanation: Alpha-cell glucagon is stimulated by low glucose, high amino acids, and intense exercise.
questions.miniGuide: Alpha-cell glucagon is stimulated by low glucose, high amino acids, and intense exercise.

questions.question: Which hepatic response is caused by glucagon?

choices.B: Increased glycogen synthesis and decreased glucose release
choices.C: Increased triglyceride storage and decreased ketogenesis
choices.D: Increased GLUT4 translocation in skeletal muscle

questions.explanation: Glucagon is a major catabolic hormone that mobilizes liver fuel and supports blood glucose between meals.
questions.miniGuide: Glucagon is a major catabolic hormone that mobilizes liver fuel and supports blood glucose between meals.

questions.question: At high levels, glucagon can produce which additional effect?

choices.C: Reduced cardiac contractile strength
choices.D: Increased triglyceride storage in the liver

questions.explanation: High glucagon can promote fat mobilization while inhibiting hepatic triglyceride storage and supporting ketone formation.
questions.miniGuide: High glucagon can promote fat mobilization while inhibiting hepatic triglyceride storage and supporting ketone formation.

questions.question: Which pancreatic cells secrete somatostatin?

choices.C: Beta cells
choices.D: Delta cells

questions.explanation: Delta cells release somatostatin in response to nutrients and gastrointestinal hormones.
questions.miniGuide: Delta cells release somatostatin in response to nutrients and gastrointestinal hormones.

questions.question: What is the overall digestive effect of pancreatic somatostatin?

choices.A: It accelerates intestinal motility and absorption.
choices.B: It increases gastric acid and pancreatic secretion.
choices.C: It selectively increases glucagon without affecting insulin.
choices.D: It slows gastrointestinal motility, secretion, and absorption.

questions.explanation: Somatostatin acts as a broad inhibitory signal, slowing gastrointestinal activity and restraining insulin and glucagon secretion.
questions.miniGuide: Somatostatin acts as a broad inhibitory signal, slowing gastrointestinal activity and restraining insulin and glucagon secretion.

questions.question: Which system provides the first broad buffer against rapid changes in blood glucose?

choices.A: The thyroid converts excess glucose into thyroid hormone.
choices.B: The kidney prevents all glucose loss regardless of concentration.
choices.C: The liver stores or releases glucose as conditions change.
choices.D: The adrenal medulla stores circulating glucose.

questions.explanation: The liver buffers blood glucose, while insulin and glucagon provide feedback control and stress hormones support prolonged counterregulation.
questions.miniGuide: The liver buffers blood glucose, while insulin and glucagon provide feedback control and stress hormones support prolonged counterregulation.

questions.question: Why is maintaining blood glucose especially important?

choices.A: The brain and certain other tissues depend heavily on glucose.
choices.B: Skeletal muscle cannot use fatty acids.
choices.C: Every tissue can use only glucose under all conditions.
choices.D: Adipose tissue cannot store any other fuel.

questions.explanation: The lecture emphasizes glucose dependence of the brain, retina, and germinal epithelium, making severe hypoglycemia dangerous.
questions.miniGuide: The lecture emphasizes glucose dependence of the brain, retina, and germinal epithelium, making severe hypoglycemia dangerous.

questions.question: How can marked hyperglycemia produce dehydration?

choices.A: Insulin directly removes water from the extracellular fluid.
choices.B: Filtered glucose raises tubular osmotic pressure and causes osmotic diuresis.
choices.C: Glucagon blocks filtration and traps water in the kidney.
choices.D: Somatostatin increases sweat production until volume falls.

questions.explanation: Excess glucose raises extracellular osmotic pressure and spills into urine, drawing water with it and contributing to cellular and extracellular dehydration.
questions.miniGuide: Excess glucose raises extracellular osmotic pressure and spills into urine, drawing water with it and contributing to cellular and extracellular dehydration.

questions.question: Diabetes mellitus involves impaired carbohydrate, fat, and protein metabolism caused by what?

choices.C: Excess somatostatin alone
choices.D: Too little insulin or reduced insulin sensitivity

questions.explanation: Diabetes results from insufficient insulin action, whether insulin is absent or target tissues respond poorly.
questions.miniGuide: Diabetes results from insufficient insulin action, whether insulin is absent or target tissues respond poorly.

questions.question: What is the central endocrine defect in type 1 diabetes mellitus?

choices.A: Loss of insulin secretion from beta cells
choices.B: Loss of somatostatin from acinar cells
choices.C: Excess glucagon secretion from delta cells
choices.D: Excess insulin secretion from alpha cells

questions.explanation: Type 1 diabetes is insulin-dependent because beta-cell destruction produces an absolute insulin deficiency.
questions.miniGuide: Type 1 diabetes is insulin-dependent because beta-cell destruction produces an absolute insulin deficiency.

questions.question: Which metabolic pattern best follows loss of insulin in type 1 diabetes?

choices.A: Reduced blood glucose with increased fat storage
choices.B: Increased glucose uptake with increased protein storage
choices.C: Hyperglycemia with increased fat and protein breakdown
choices.D: Reduced lipolysis with reduced ketone production

questions.explanation: Absolute insulin deficiency impairs glucose use while accelerating catabolism, contributing to fat loss, protein wasting, and possible ketogenesis.
questions.miniGuide: Absolute insulin deficiency impairs glucose use while accelerating catabolism, contributing to fat loss, protein wasting, and possible ketogenesis.

questions.question: Which feature is most characteristic of type 2 diabetes mellitus?

choices.A: Autoimmune loss of all pancreatic cell types
choices.C: Insulin resistance often associated with obesity
choices.D: Complete absence of glucagon from birth

questions.explanation: Type 2 diabetes is characterized primarily by reduced tissue sensitivity to insulin and is commonly preceded by obesity.
questions.miniGuide: Type 2 diabetes is characterized primarily by reduced tissue sensitivity to insulin and is commonly preceded by obesity.

questions.question: Which cluster best represents metabolic syndrome?

choices.A: Low glucagon, low cortisol, and reduced sympathetic activity
choices.B: Low body weight, high insulin sensitivity, and hypoglycemia
choices.C: Adrenal failure, salt wasting, and hyperkalemia
choices.D: Central obesity, insulin resistance, hyperglycemia, and lipid abnormalities

questions.explanation: Metabolic syndrome groups central obesity and insulin resistance with impaired glucose control, abnormal lipids, and related cardiovascular risk.
questions.miniGuide: Metabolic syndrome groups central obesity and insulin resistance with impaired glucose control, abnormal lipids, and related cardiovascular risk.

questions.question: What does glycated hemoglobin primarily reflect?

choices.A: Blood glucose at the exact moment of testing
choices.B: Pancreatic insulin stores after one meal
choices.C: Glucagon secretion during an overnight fast
choices.D: Average blood glucose over roughly three months

questions.explanation: Glucose remains attached to hemoglobin over the red cell's lifespan, allowing A1C to estimate longer-term glycemic exposure.
questions.miniGuide: Glucose remains attached to hemoglobin over the red cell's lifespan, allowing A1C to estimate longer-term glycemic exposure.

questions.question: During an oral glucose-tolerance test, which response is most consistent with diabetes?

choices.B: Glucose returns rapidly to resting level.
choices.C: Glucose remains elevated for four to six hours.
choices.D: Glucose immediately falls below fasting level.

questions.explanation: Persistent elevation after a glucose load indicates impaired regulation rather than the normal return toward resting values.
questions.miniGuide: Persistent elevation after a glucose load indicates impaired regulation rather than the normal return toward resting values.

questions.question: What is the major immediate danger of an insulin-secreting islet adenoma?

choices.C: Severe hyperglycemia from absent insulin
choices.D: Hyperkalemia from absent aldosterone

questions.explanation: An insulinoma can cause hyperinsulinism; progressively lower glucose may produce trembling, neurologic dysfunction, seizures, loss of consciousness, or coma.
questions.miniGuide: An insulinoma can cause hyperinsulinism; progressively lower glucose may produce trembling, neurologic dysfunction, seizures, loss of consciousness, or coma.

questions.question: Which comparison of type 1 and type 2 diabetes is correct?

choices.A: Both begin with complete absence of insulin secretion.
choices.B: Type 1 features absolute insulin deficiency, while type 2 initially features insulin resistance.
choices.C: Type 1 begins with insulin resistance, while type 2 begins with beta-cell destruction.
choices.D: Type 1 affects only fat metabolism, while type 2 affects only carbohydrate metabolism.

questions.explanation: Both disorders impair carbohydrate, fat, and protein metabolism, but their central defects differ: beta-cell insulin loss in type 1 versus reduced tissue responsiveness in type 2.
questions.miniGuide: Both disorders impair carbohydrate, fat, and protein metabolism, but their central defects differ: beta-cell insulin loss in type 1 versus reduced tissue responsiveness in type 2.
